newsitem.title: UK: China's mark Eurobond attracts strong demand.
newsitem.headline: China's mark Eurobond attracts strong demand.

text.p: An investor scramble to buy China's first Eurobond this year left the 500 million mark ($290 million) deal heavily oversubscribed on Thursday.
"We were three to four times oversubscribed," an official at joint lead manager Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said. "We have no bonds left, and people are really trying to get hold of them."
China last tapped the international bond markets in July 1996, when it issued dollar transactions. It has no outstanding mark Eurobonds.

"China created a kind of collector's item by keeping the size of the deal so small," the Deutsche official said. "It is the only bond available from the People's Republic in marks, so for many investors it is the only way to get this kind of diversification."

Deutsche said the bonds were bought by a broad mix of investors. Around a quarter went to retail investors, and mutual fund managers, central banks and bank asset allocation departments were also buyers.
About one-third of the paper was sold in Germany, with 30 percent going to Asia accounts, and 30 percent placed in Britain, Deutsche said.
China priced the bond to yield 55 basis points over German government paper. By 1130 GMT it had traded in by one or two notches.
In May China's credit rating was upgraded by Standard and Poor's to BBB+, and is rated A3 by Moody's.
Investor focus is also on the handover of Hong Kong to China -- now only 12 days away.
At a presentation to bankers in London this week, China said it wanted to establish itself with European investors ahead of the planned single currency.

Other objectives of the transaction were to set a benchmark and to fund infrastructure projects, Zhu Guang Yao, deputy director general of the state debt management department of the Ministry of Finance said.
China issued $1.0 billion worth of bonds in 1996, and Zhu said that this year borrowing would not exceed that.
